entries.test: Publicly documented Copilot achievement summaries and their underlying records would show whether it invents achievements, metrics, or supporting citations.
entries.note: Zitron adopts the source's finding in his own voice.
The sentence primarily judges Microsoft's culture through the evaluative terms “subservience” and “abusive pseudoscience.”

entries.test: Public documentation of Microsoft's employment decisions would show whether Copilot summaries used for reward or promotion justifications lead to AI determining hiring or firing decisions.
entries.note: The proposition converts a prediction about what Microsoft will likely say its policy prohibits into an unqualified statement of that policy. The ultimate employment-decision forecast is firm.
The prediction concerns companies meeting a stated antecedent. “Given up on managing,” maximal automation, and judgment by managers' “whims” do not supply a shared test for membership or outcome.

entries.test: Contemporaneous Microsoft disclosures or documented code-production records would show whether its AI-written code share was close to Google's claimed 25% at publication.
entries.note: “I anticipate” expresses an expectation about the present here, rather than a mere possibility or a dated future prediction.

entries.test: Comparisons of class declarations produced for the same requirements by AI models and conventional IDE completion would show whether their functional outputs differ materially.
entries.note: The surrounding text identifies the relevant comparison as the resulting code.

entries.test: Public examples or audits of Google's AI-generated code at publication would show whether it was confined to comments and tests or included substantive software functionality.
entries.note: The follow-up assertion endorses the second alternative in the question. “Fairly confident” expresses affirmative confidence rather than merely suggesting a possibility.
This evaluates the worth of a metric for judging software work.

entries.test: Public records of business or operational collapse at the companies described, together with technical investigations, would show whether failure followed dependence on automated, error-ridden infrastructure.
entries.note: The language is colorful, but the prediction of eventual collapse is categorical and has no deadline.

entries.test: Microsoft's growth records and public evidence of its management practices and reform decisions would show whether continued growth sustains the criticized workplace practices.
entries.note: “Things” refers in context to the management culture just described. The causal assertion includes an undated prediction of persistence.

entries.test: Public reporting and company records would show whether Microsoft's described management and AI-mediated performance-review system breaks down or is abandoned because it fails.
entries.note: The contextual target is the described corporate setup; the passage does not specifically predict bankruptcy. “It has to” makes the prediction firm despite the metaphor.
